name: Yusuf Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so tell me both what you would say openly and what you really think. What happens during a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Yusuf, 43, an experienced developer at a tech company that tracks chilled-food deliveries. I have a bachelor’s degree and handle ordinary temperature-alert code, while a specialist handles the hardest sensor failures. I check overnight alerts, compare them with the driver’s temperature sheet, and fix the logic before another load leaves. I use AI now and then to summarise alert logs after colleagues have tried it, but I still check the readings myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the family side of this job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Hana, runs a small home bakery, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My developer pay is high for this job, and we have about nine months of expenses saved. There are plenty of similar jobs nearby. Hana’s cake orders rise and fall by season, so we keep her business money separate from mortgage cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AI Plateau leaves us checking that cold food actually stayed cold. A shorter alert summary is useful, but it cannot replace the driver’s temperature sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would feel secure about my job and the mortgage. Nine months saved protects us from a slow bakery season while my developer pay holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking AI log summaries against driver sheets and ask the specialist to review odd sensor gaps. I’d continue moving 450 monthly into household savings while my pay stays high. In the first year I’d show Hana how I compare the alerts with the thermometer readings in her bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the main wage, though I still care when food spoils. The small AI change does not look like a threat to our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which alert taught you to check paper records?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A truck once reported a safe temperature after the sensor stopped sending readings. The driver’s paper temperature sheet showed a blank hour the truck dashboard called safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the bakery buy a new monitor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show Hana the blank-hour example, but I would not buy a new monitor for the bakery without seeing a recurring problem. Her current thermometer still works.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave people checking cold-food records.
I would preserve **driver sheets** beside shorter alert summaries.
think: I expect my **developer pay** to stay secure.
Our **nine-month cushion** covers a slow bakery season while my wage holds.
do: **Keep** comparing AI log summaries with driver temperature sheets.
**Transfer** 450 monthly into household savings while developer pay remains high.
**Show** Hana how to check blank alert hours against bakery thermometer readings.
feel: **Calm** about bills, with concern for spoiled food.
S0.quote: The driver’s paper temperature sheet showed a blank hour the truck dashboard called safe.
fieldNote: His **occasional AI use** is limited to log summaries checked against physical readings.
High pay and **nine months saved** protect the mortgage during variable bakery orders.

steps.text: Keep comparing chilled-delivery alert summaries against driver sheets
Transfer 450 monthly to household savings while developer pay holds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will let software draft alerts, plan routes and answer customers faster. I would ask our drivers to test any new temperature checker before we reduce human review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think our team might need fewer developers, and I could lose hours. Hana’s bakery could also get cheaper automated booking, though the baking itself stays hands-on longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d test the approved assistant on eighteen old sensor-gap cases with a driver and the specialist. If it spots every gap, I’d learn to review its alerts during paid work time. In the first year, if my hours are cut, Hana and I would pause the bakery’s planned delivery advertising and keep the cash for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because a pay cut could arrive while bakery orders are already uneven. Nine months of savings is a buffer, not a reason to ignore the risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which alert would judge the assistant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the driver the case where the sensor fell silent but the screen stayed green. If the assistant misses it, the old manual check stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really stop the bakery advertising?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Hana to compare actual paid orders with the advertising cost before stopping it. We should not cut something that brings in more than it costs.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to speed alerts, routes and customer replies.
I would require **driver-tested checks** before reducing human review.
think: I worry **developer hours** may shrink if routine alert checks move to the new software.
I expect bakery **booking software** to change before hands-on baking, adding pressure to Hana’s orders.
do: **Test** an approved assistant on eighteen old sensor gaps this month.
**Learn** its alert review during paid time only if all gaps are found.
**Pause** bakery advertising if my hours fall and paid orders do not cover its cost.
feel: **Anxious** about code pay and uneven bakery orders.
S1.quote: I would ask our drivers to test any new temperature checker before we reduce human review.
fieldNote: His **eighteen-case test** and paid-time learning come before any reduction in manual checks.
Bakery **advertising stops** only after lost hours and evidence that orders fail to cover its cost.

steps.text: Learn approved alert review during paid time if eighteen old gaps are found

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AGI by 2028 can do our cold-chain code thinking work in 2028. Robots for hands-on work arrive around 2031, so Hana’s baking may have more time than my desk job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect most alert-code roles could disappear, including mine. Nine months saved helps, but bakery bookings might also be automated and our mortgage will keep coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the company for written severance and hold off on buying Hana’s proposed second oven. I’d keep the oven money with our reserve and list real local jobs rather than assume a developer vacancy survives. In the first year after 2028, if dismissed, I’d apply for actual openings and use savings for essentials while we search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I expect a large loss of my pay. A second bakery oven would be the wrong place to hold our cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say about the second oven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Hana the current oven can carry the orders we already have. We would buy a second only if paid orders justify it after our income is clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would family help carry the search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not ask Hana to work every night to replace my wage. I would ask my mother for two afternoons of childcare during interviews only if she is free.

say: I expect **AGI by 2028** to reach alert code before baking robots arrive.
I would tell colleagues Hana’s **hands-on baking** may change later.
think: I expect my **code role** could disappear.
Our **nine-month savings** cannot guarantee bakery bookings or a replacement job.
do: **Delay** buying a second oven and hold the cash for bills now.
**Request** written severance and identify actual local job openings.
**Apply** for real vacancies if dismissed after 2028, asking my mother for childcare if free.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected lost pay despite a nine-month reserve.
S2.quote: A second bakery oven would be the wrong place to hold our cash.
fieldNote: He faces the **2028 code shock** before robots around 2031 reach hands-on baking.
His **mother’s childcare** depends on availability; a second oven requires paid orders after income is clear.

steps.text: Delay buying a second bakery oven and hold its cash
Apply for actual local jobs if dismissed after 2028
Ask mother for interview childcare only if she is free

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives five years to understand what chilled deliveries still need from people. Thinking AI reaches our code in 2031; hands-on robots arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect fewer code jobs, but I can learn how drivers verify a temperature gap while I earn. I will not assume the field checks remain a paid job after robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d spend one approved morning monthly with a driver learning how a paper sheet is checked after a sensor gap. I’d use the free food-safety guide if my manager refuses the time. In the first year after 2031, if coding work ends, I’d apply only for real cold-chain support jobs whose pay covers our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my role, but I have time to test another skill. Hana and I would keep the oven money until actual orders make the decision clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you show a field skill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the driver to mark one gap report I wrote each month. If the explanation misses an hour, I need more practice before claiming field skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not pay for a safety certificate without a real vacancy requiring it. The free guide and a marked report show me where I stand.

say: I see **AGI by 2031** as time to study chilled-delivery checks.
I know **2034 robots** follow the earlier code change.
think: I expect **fewer coding jobs** despite more warning.
I cannot assume **field checks** stay paid once robots arrive.
do: **Learn** driver gap checks monthly with marked-report feedback if manager approves time.
**Study** the free food-safety guide if approved time is refused.
**Apply** for real mortgage-paying cold-chain jobs if coding ends after 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about my job, with a chance to test a skill.
S3.quote: I will not assume the field checks remain a paid job after robots arrive.
fieldNote: His **five-year plan** builds marked reports while acknowledging robots may later replace field checks.
The **driver morning** needs approval; a role change needs a vacancy and sufficient pay.

steps.text: Learn monthly gap checks with driver-marked reports if approved; otherwise use free food-safety guide
Apply for actual cold-chain jobs covering mortgage if coding ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives a decade to improve chilled-food safety and train newer staff. Thinking AI reaches code in 2036; robots for hands-on work arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my pay to hold in the next few years and the bakery to keep its customers. I still would not put the family reserve into equipment without paid demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep comparing sensor alerts with driver sheets and save 450 monthly while my pay holds. I’d help Hana trial a small weekly order list using the current oven, with no new lease or equipment. In the first year after 2036, we would continue that order list only if repeat paid orders cover ingredients and delivery time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about future work, but our present bills feel secure. I can test a ten-order bakery list without making the mortgage pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the order trial worth keeping?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cap the weekly list at ten orders and count actual payment, not messages asking for prices. If it loses money for two months, we would stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would do the extra work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hana would bake and I would handle the weekend delivery only if it fits our children’s schedule. We would not make the children run the business for us.

I know **2039 robots** follow the earlier code change.
think: I expect my **pay and bakery income** to hold near term.
I will not put **family savings** into equipment without paid demand.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my code pay could go before we know whether the bakery can support us. Written severance, paid time to learn driver checks and real vacancies would help. My mother could cover two interview afternoons if she is free, but her savings are not ours.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs for a spoiled load when the dashboard says the truck stayed cold. A green cold-chain alert cannot put spoiled food back on the shelf.

headlineQuote: A green cold-chain alert cannot put spoiled food back on the shelf.
portrait: Yusuf is a **43-year-old mid-level developer** with a bachelor’s degree, high pay and nine months of expenses saved.
He uses **AI occasionally** for chilled-delivery summaries, checking them against driver sheets and sensor gaps.
His partner’s **home bakery** has seasonal paid orders; hands-on baking faces robots later than his code.
He limits **business trials** to the current oven and paid demand while seeking approved field learning and real vacancies.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his code income before the bakery proves it can support the mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: **Written severance**, paid driver-check learning and actual openings would help.
